utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there are no preliminaries. Therefore, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time for the following issues: First, housekeeping session. The Chamber would like to reserve the first session of tomorrow for the housekeeping session. Furthermore, should the accused wish to waive his right to be present during this first session, the Defence should inform the Registry so as to co-ordinate transport from the UNDU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind that you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we discussed the report from San Antonio.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please have that on our screens again, 65 ter 2008 [as interpreted]. We need page 4 in e-court in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were discussing the comments that your colleagues had in view of the proceedings that took place in Bosnia. In number 8 -- actually, could we have the next page, please, page 5 in e-court. Mr. Peerwani was mentioned. Did Mr. Peerwani work in Bosnia as well? We know that he was with you in Rwanda. Was he in Bosnia as well?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was in Bosnia also. I'd have to look that up. I believe he did though.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us please go back to page 4 now. Number 5, you've already explained that to us that the gentleman is a good friend of yours, Dr. Clyde Snow. And you said that he was critical of your work. Mr. Snow, or, rather, Dr. Snow said that you worked against time and against -- or, rather, verse the UNTAES. Did you have an opportunity of discussing that with him; namely, what he meant by that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really sure he meant by that. He wasn't involved in the exhumations or anything like that. I never talked to him. This came up a long time after -- after the work in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tom Grow, number 6. He was not critical either towards you or Dr. Kirschner. You are under number 7. You complained about time, resources, and security. You said that they were too limited.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well these things sort of happened. We are not in the United States, and we don't have that -- we do what we have to do, you know. So those things happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you have all the information -- or, rather, did you know about the problem that was created by Dr. Kirschner, that is to say, at the time when you were heard, before this commission?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pretty much came up during this situation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you did not mention that problem, or did you mention it and it was not recorded nevertheless? Do you remember which one of the two would be correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here, we cannot see that you criticised Dr. Kirschner. So now I'm asking you whether you did indeed criticise him?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's not here, I didn't criticise him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm a bit surprised by the use of the word "testimony." Do you mean during the interview or -- because testimony is a formal statement given in court which is, at least here, always recorded in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the term I find in previous transcripts. They called this procedure testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's clear to me now what you were referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I asked you whether you had information before you were heard by this commission about Dr. Kirschner's actions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have, but I don't -- I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you consider establishing the causes of death something of importance for your investigation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was up to the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Precisely those who were directly under Dr. Kirschner's control; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they worked with him. I don't know how much control that was involved in that, but they all worked together, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll be jumping back now, if you will. Could we please see page 4 again. Dr. Andrew Thomson, we see what he says. In the last sentence, it is stated -- or, rather, he says -- he speaks of Dr. Kirschner as losing control of himself.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he certainly -- I think he was ill, and I think that he was having problems. That's basically, you know ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Witness, you said, "Well, he certainly," and then you stopped. You referred to him being ill and having problems. And then you said, "That's basically, you know ...," but we don't know. Could you please complete the two sentences I just read to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he had to go back to the United States quite a lot. Subsequently he died, and he had been ill for a long time, so I think that may have been part of, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could I ask you, the criticism that you -- this does not -- it describes the mental state of the person, but it's not a response to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when a person is very ill, oftentimes they lose a little of the dimensions of what they are doing or what they have do, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you say you establish, in your opinion, a link between Dr. Kirschner losing control of himself with his illness. The first question, of course, is whether you agree that he lost control of himself. And then the second question would be the explanation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see that he'd really lost control of himself, but I know he was gone a lot, which made it difficult for some of the other pathologists and -- and partially for himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you can't confirm that he lost control of himself and, under those circumstances, of course, to speculate on the reasons why, but you could consider that if he did, that it would have been -- perhaps be related to his condition at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. But we had pathologists back there that held things together and continued with the work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under 9 and 10, two colleagues who are archaeologists are referred to. They also do not mention at all Dr. Kirschner. Did they have any contact with him? Do you know whether archaeologists had any kind of contact with Dr. Kirschner?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, when in the laboratory, each autopsy, the anthropologist determined the average age of the individuals, measured bones that -- made note of the height, just various dimensions sometimes that would help or at least would put those kinds of -- those individuals, and those heights and things like that that will help and further on help in the identification of the individuals so it would -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree about the anthropologists. However, it says here that these persons are archaeologists. What about archaeologists? Did they work on this identification? Did they have encounters, if you will, with Dr. Kirschner?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no. I got no information that there were any problems like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 11, Mr. Patrick Meyers. He criticised you, your absence, and he claims that you compromised the locations there. Did you talk to Mr. Meyers afterwards? Did you try to clarify matters in terms of this criticism that he had voiced? Please take a look at number 11.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could make this a little larger, it would make it easier to read it. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Just number 11.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand the -- the -- the -- what he was saying. There was flooding in a grave. And I'm not another sure what grave he is talking about so it would be difficult for me to answer this question from him. I didn't get very many people that said things like this. But everyone has their own way of observation and thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Number 12, Yvonne Milewski, was interviewed. She supported you but she's one of the persons who said that she was instructed by Dr. Kirschner as to how to list the cause of death. On the ground, were you informed by people who complained about this? Actually, at the time when all of this was happening, did anyone on the ground tell you that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is between the pathologists and Dr. Kirschner, not between me. I didn't know about this until I -- until I saw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 13, Dorothy Gallagher, who is an anthropologist -- who is an anthropologist like you. She says that she saw problems in the field and in the lab.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we went over this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just have a few additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said before, because the translation continued when he was speaking. Mr. Lukic asked you, he said that she saw problems in the field and in the lab. What you did then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we answered this, I think, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'm just asking you to repeat what you said a second ago. Is that you referred to yesterday's testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So Ms. Gallagher claimed that Dr. Kirschner changed reports himself and also that he instructed her to do so while processing the reports. My question for you is: How much time did she spend in you -- in Bosnia working with you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how long she was there. I didn't keep track of when people came in and out. Just so there was enough people. I don't know how long she was there. I know that they -- people were there and that's what made most for me -- you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection she had been there for a couple of weeks or a couple of months or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh yeah, a couple -- a couple -- a couple of -- she may have been there a month or maybe over. She wasn't there a long time but she was there at least a month, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic kindly speak into the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next person, number 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to speak into the microphone by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm a bit stretched.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] David del Pino, also an anthropologist is number 14. He is from Chile. Again, he criticised you. He said that clothing was discarded, clothing on the basis of which identification could have been performed. You explained that, that clothing was discarded. Now I'd just like to ask you whether you would agree with me on the following: Namely, that South American anthropologists [Realtime transcript read in error "pathologists"], and Mr. del Pino is from South America, are far more qualified in this field than the same experts from the US.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was just one person who was not an American. There was an awful lot of other ones that didn't say anything and didn't have any problem with that so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question, however, was whether South American pathologists -- whether they are far more qualified in this field than the same experts from the United States. Whether they were there or not is another question but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were anthropologists and not pathologists. And just like everybody else, they have different -- they have done different grave, et cetera, and that ... he could complain about that, that was -- other people didn't, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. [In English] Can you just listen to the question posed by Presiding Judge Orie, please. The question was whether South American anthropologists are more qualified than the US anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were more qualified with mass graves. In the United States maybe archeologists did some ancient graves, but -- you'd be very, very -- you wouldn't see -- I hadn't seen any mass graves in the United States for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are also some other objections. Would you agree that uniform forms were not used regularly in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the procedures that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- there's not a much that can you do in the field. You want to make sure that you get the right bodies and the right number, et cetera, and then you dig more, and you get the remains to the point where you can take them out and you dig some more. This was gathered -- and I kept -- when I was there, and other people -- the idea was how many people we got, what -- what any -- what -- any special things that we needed to put down on, and it's all in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But were uniform forms used or not, or was it...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There -- if there were I would have left those in the reports, and they're not, no. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kept notes, but I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 7 in the same version of the document, please, where we have the findings of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of the work that was done, you were in charge of administration and logistics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much of the administration was also done by the other doctor that you just mentioned a bit ago, Andrew. And -- so he was dealing with the -- with the Tribunal, and -- and doing much of that too. So he was -- he might help you, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was "also done by the other doctor." Is that to be understood as that you did much of it as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. But he -- when he was not around, then I dealt with the -- with the Tribunal also. But he was supposed to be in the -- most of the time he was dealing with the -- with the Tribunal and getting those things done. It made it easier. But I did deal with the Tribunal also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had Mr. Andrew Thomson in mind?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And he is the one that actually got me involved with the -- with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic so as to avoid any confusion, your question was about administration and logistics. Did you intend to ask about Tribunal business because the answer is mainly about who dealt with Tribunal business? If that is what you intended to ask, then, if not, please then make your question more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any other administrative and logistical work, save your relationship with the Tribunal? In other words, what was your understanding of administration and logistics in the course of the work that was performed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in charge of doing the exhumations and that's basically what I did, but I oftentimes they would -- they would ask me to deal with the media down in Bosnia and -- when we were there. And sometimes they would -- once or twice, maybe, they came by just to see what kind of work we did from the Tribunal, a couple of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, I understand logistics to be to provide the necessary means you need to do your job such as materials you would need, transportation of the bodies, et cetera. That's what I understand to be logistics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was whether you were involved in the logistics, or whether you left that to others. That's the question I take it, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I work with Andrew also. But to get things to us, he was back in -- in The Hague and we were dealing with an American group that would help, that was helping. [Indiscernible] not at the point, no. But getting things for us, he could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he did -- he did it, not you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We both worked on those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, matters such as transportation of the bodies to the morgue, were those logistical matters also dealt with by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that part of the logistics you organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the report, on page 7, we see that according to the commission -- please bear with me. In line 5 we find the following in the English version, as well as in the B/C/S, on page 7, just under findings: "Rather, it became apparent that the main problems with the exhumations were administrative and logistic."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were any problem, yeah, it would fall on that, yeah. I'm not sure what exactly this was about, yeah. But if were there problems, yeah, we were dealing with them or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the extent you were in charge of administration and logistics who did the commission learn of these problems from? You say there could have been issues. But who could have presented the issues to them so that they were able to arrive at this conclusion that the basic problems were in the field of administration and logistics?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you'd have to talk to the people in -- at the -- here, actually. They're the ones that went and had this done, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you did not bring out the administrative and logistics problems before the commission in the sense of the problems you encountered in the field.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day things come up. Most -- all the time is pretty minor. You don't take this to something like this. I answered questions that these individuals were asking and -- and I was able to go through what I do, and how I did, and they were sort of amazed that we got through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you brief people upon their arrival on location in terms of what was needed to be done?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, people did get -- we sat down and -- and -- not -- they only work with other individuals. I partnered them up with other people so that they'd catch on what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a work-plan, an operation plan, that the people were acquainted with?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not, I don't think of in a real rigid sort of situation. You learn things, that is, as you go along, and a lot of the people I knew that came in, they knew what to do. They just needed to know how we were actually doing it and how we would get along in doing it and getting things done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since, under item 1 in the chapter findings, it is stated that there were no systematic briefings at the sites upon arrival, and it seems that no one has been given any standard plan of operation. Would you agree with this part of the commission findings?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we didn't have a sit-down, we should have done, and we find out later years that other things are happening. You do that. You sit down and go through things. I don't know how they did with the continuation of other graves and that. But, yes, that is something that you do, and I learned that from a -- and subsequently did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were people aware of what kind of chain of responsibility there was? Was that concept involved at all?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I pretty much the people knew what -- what to do, and they knew how to do it. I don't think there was a problem in that, in my mind anyway. Most of the people just got to work. They had much experience. We didn't have to really teach them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you would not agree with the -- this finding of the commission. Towards the end of paragraph 1, it seems that the commission finds that there was no clear concept of the chain of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of -- well, that -- that was their -- their -- they felt -- they felt that it should be -- they came from -- you know, they were in -- most of the United States or Canada. They had very solid things of what they do and everybody could do. I mean, I wrote all the -- the -- how actually everything would happen when I worked in -- in the medical examiner's office, but there was nothing written for something like that. It's a great idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't think it was as rugged as it seems like because most of the persons did their work. You didn't see a majority of these people that were working. You didn't see them on this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, in your view, did the people know who was the person in charge, who was supposed to issue tasks, and who held responsibility? Was that described to them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are people that knew what they were doing. They didn't have to be told every day what to do, how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Briefly only, I'd like to look at 1D1158, which is your testimony in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 51. Actually, let's start with page 49 because that is where we find the question, and the answer is a rather long one. Line 5. It has to do with this particular item. I'll quote: [In English] "Q. Do you agree with the findings -- "A. Of ... "Q. -- contained in paragraph 1, and not just because they found it, I'm asking you personally, sir, do you agree with this? "A. Not in total." And now if we can jump to page 51 in the e-court, it should be transcript page 8949, line 15 to 18. I quote: "A. Well, the people didn't understand who was in charge, I guess it might be my fault. "Q. Might be? "A. Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, do you accept this part of your testimony given in the Popovic case as accurate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it -- if that's what it said, that's what I said. I almost want to say something, but I don't think I can. I don't know if I should say something, but I'm having a lot of memory loss and it's really difficult for me to remember things and bringing them up. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's appropriate to tell us that. Is there any specific reason why you are suffering from a memory loss at this moment? Is there any illness involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is -- this is -- yeah. I could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. If you'd prefer to discuss that, which is a private matter, not in public, then we would move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you prefer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we could do it. I think we could do it. I don't think I'm doing very well here and I'm just grabbing for things, and I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Dr. Haglund, when you testified before this Tribunal at previous occasions, did you always answer the questions to the best of your recollection and as accurately as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we take a break now. And you'll be escorted out of the courtroom. Would 20 minutes be enough? Or would you like to have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's fine. I'm ready to do whatever I need to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But also what you're capable of doing. We don't want you to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- do more than you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to give the following decision: The Chamber formally admits the following documents into evidence which are already marked in e-court as having been admitted but we still have to formally admit them. That's P1528, P1633, P1641, and P1652, among them, P1641 is under seal. Have the parties reached any conclusions as how to -- they would preferably proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I ... Mr. McCloskey is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We spoke about the possibility of offering a more detailed testimony, and -- and spoke of the -- the Popovic case as being the most complete with a very extensive cross-examination, and so -- but that's -- that's where we left it. And we're open to -- to getting together and -- and deciding on what portions of that testimony to -- to provide you with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, that is the common position of the parties. Because the Chamber would be reluctant to allow for any further examination of the witness where he would have to rely on his memory in answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then further cross is not possible, of course, if he cannot rely on his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I don't -- and I'm not a doctor, but I -- I think it's -- if Mr. Haglund, if we could consult him on that I -- you know, none of our memories are perfect. He could try, and if it is obviously impossible, then, of course, there would be -- we would not be left with any option. I am concerned that if cross-examination is stopped prematurely, then that throws in the ability to provide these documents in some question. His crucial reports in that work that was done that we get into the issues does that make him unavailable, 92 quater, complicated legal issues, whereas we're almost done, and he has done his best, and I think he has just alerted you that, you know, he is not a young man and got some issues. But I think he is trying. And there's a massive record for Mr. Lukic to deal with, and a wonderful cross-examination record for many case, so I don't think we're at a stage -- I would ask that we continue to try and get through this. And if Dr. Haglund can't answer questions, he'll tell us. Or, of course, of course, if you don't feel you're getting the kind of courtroom -- and testimony that you need, that's absolutely -- and I understand absolutely in your discretion and prerogative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber allows you to continue, but, at the same time, urges you to keep in mind what you would ask the witness and where -- what kind of questions you would put to him. You have to consider that. And for you, Mr. Haglund, whenever you feel that your recollection is -- is not sufficient to answer the question, don't hesitate to tell us immediately. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to inform you either I will have full cross, I cannot have semi-cross. I will ask the questions to test the memory. That's my right. And if you expect me to do something in between, I cannot do that. So my questions will be directed to test previous statements and documents and previous statements of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber does not deny the right of the Defence to put questions to the witness as the Defence deems fit. The instruction to Mr. Haglund remains the same, that if he feels that his recollection is not allowing him to answer the question, that he should tell us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Again, we need 65 ter 20008. That's the report of the San Antonio Committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you misspoke or it is a translation issue. It is 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's recorded properly, 20008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently there is some disagreement. Let's see what appears on our screen and see whether that's the document we'd like to have, and then we'll see in e-court ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll check in e-court and we'll find out if it's 20008. At least that what Madam Registrar tells me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm always thankful to Judge Fluegge for reminding us of our mistakes of numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And if I made a mistake, I would like to refer to page 2, line 4. I took the number 2008. That was wrong at the outset of today's hearing. But we now agree that we have the right document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 10 in this document. Opinions and comments is the heading. In brackets: (Dr. DiMaio). And it says here that the actions of Dr. Kirschner in regard to the changing of the cause and manner of death in select cases without prior approval notification or consultation with the individuals who actually performed the autopsies is not acceptable conduct. However, now we know that that is beyond dispute. Let us look at the last sentence in this paragraph where it says: "His subsequent actions in discarding worksheets from the autopsy reports in which he made changes, while apparently done without malice, compounds his original mistake and was totally inappropriate." Do you know that Mr. Kirschner, at the time, physically changed files, or, rather, concealed pages and inserted other corrected ones?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall knowing anything about that at all until this happened. I think all the answers are in this ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I'd like to move on to Roman numeral IX, discussion and conclusions. In the B/C/S version, we need the last paragraph on page 10 and in the English version, the first line on page 11. I'm going to ask you whether you agree with some of these conclusions. What is written here is the following: "There was mutual agreement on management problems on the part of the supervisors." You were one of the supervisors; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to yourself who was else was a supervisor because we see the plural here?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when -- when Dr. Kirschner was gone, other people had taken his place. He'd appoint people to do that, take his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did he leave? From when did he no longer take part in this work? Or did he actually complete this work at these locations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I -- I -- I just can't answer that one. I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know until when Dr. Kirschner worked with you in the field?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never worked with me in the field. He always worked in the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know until when Dr. Kirschner worked in a laboratory while you were working in the field?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow him around and see what he did every day and how he had to go -- and as long as it was working in the laboratory, it was fine, okay? So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for tormenting you. But when did you complete your work in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to look through these to tell you exactly what ... I read all these over, but I -- I don't remember what I read over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a minute and check this for us. Please check until when you worked in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If I can be of any help, the period is specified on page 4 of Dr. Haglund's CV. And it provides - I don't know if Dr. Haglund can confirm - that he worked there from July to November of 1996, or that at least he was engaged in -- in -- in that work, for that time-period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. And that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember that from July until November Dr. Kirschner worked with you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the laboratory a lot of times and a lot of times he had to do other things, and he left. I didn't keep track of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he put other people in his place when he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In these conclusions, again, there is a reference to lack of communication or lack of a chain of command. Would you agree with these findings of the committee or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- there -- there -- this is what they thought. I don't necessarily have to agree with all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Precisely. That's what I'm asking you, whether this conclusion of theirs actually portrays the situation on the ground; is it right? If you don't think it's right, please tell us what you think.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't think it was that way, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did people know who the volunteers worked for and were there volunteers on the ground. And did people know who they worked for?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I always thought they did, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then they we could conclude that conclusion number 2 in this report is not correct either because it says lack of information as to who the volunteers were working for.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is their -- these are people that had very good laboratories and that and everything was very solid. I felt that we were dealing with the people that worked for us and you can see there's 40 or 50 people that are not even in here, so they didn't have a problem at all so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you have a right to disagree with the report, and that is why I'm asking you. Because I wish to say that in some segments they are not right, that you are more familiar with the situation on the ground. So if you disagree, tell me, I disagree with their finding. And that's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly don't agree with all of their findings. I found out something that was happening that I wasn't even aware of. Some of this I thought was very good. They had a very good talk with me at the end and they were surprised that we were able to do as much as we could and did a good job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did people on the ground know that this was a criminal investigation because they were employed by the Office of the Prosecutor of the international Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who -- who was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: People on the ground who worked with you. Did they know that this was a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they did. But they weren't under the Tribunal. They were being -- the small pay that they got and their travel and that was done by the Physicians for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: People who worked on the ground, did they include persons who were employees of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They weren't -- they weren't involved with the PHR. But we had some people from the Tribunal, and the majority of the people were sent by Physicians for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the question; namely, would you agree that they knew that this was a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people on ground? I don't -- I don't believe so. The ones they called up to -- to -- that -- that they could talk to, they would know about it. I'm not sure about all the other people knowing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the parties' attention to page 29, line 19, where the transcript reads "They weren't involved with the PHR." That's not, I think, what the witness said. I think he said they were not involved with the Tribunal but we -- although some. The majority of the people were sent by Physicians for Human Rights and I think that should be reflected in the first line of the answer as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I will have to call up 1D1158. That's the transcript from the Popovic trial. We'll need page 6. However, it's the second part because the system could not take in the entire transcript. So it's the second part of the transcript. I just see what page this is, whether this would be the right part. Obviously I've been informed that in e-court there is a sort of an attachment because the entire transcript could not fit in. 8959 is the page. It's page 6 in other part of the transcript. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to the previous question, Doctor, in the Popovic trial, you were asked this same question. I'm going to refer to it now. [In English] "Q. So you disagree with that? "A. --"

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my previous testimonies. Right here I'm not standing by them very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Popovic case, you said it was hard for you to believe that people on the ground did not know that this was a criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you were asked whether one of the reasons why these persons had not been informed about the type of work involved was that you, as the main supervisor, never informed them fully. Did you inform people on the ground about the type of work involved?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there an answer to this in the other testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But today you don't remember what you answered; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very wavery for me to make these kind -- to answer these. I stand by these because that's when my memory was well, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't see much use of this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As long as Dr. Haglund's willing to try, I -- we -- we must take people as we find them. We find ourselves here in 2013 because the accused was on the run for several years. And no one can be perfect. There's no such thing as a perfect witness. If Dr. Haglund continues to try, I will support him. If he has had enough, I -- I will stand down. But we don't have any perfect witnesses. No one has a perfect memory. All we can ask him to do is try, which he is doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may respond shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Stakic case in front of this Tribunal, Judge Schomberg ruled that everybody has the right to run and it has nothing to do with this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone has the right to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To run.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And to hide, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that Mr. McCloskey said that the accused had no right to do that but that it has consequences. That is how -- what I understood, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Exactly. I understand why someone runs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But, again, it has nothing to do with this cross-examination, and I don't think that we can finalise this cross-examination. That's my true belief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness is available for cross-examination. Consider what you would like to ask him. And we'll listen to the answers, and we'll see how it develops. The Chamber is not ruling that cross-examination is not further possible. It's in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there a lack of communication between those supervising, that is to say, you and Dr. Kirschner on the ground, and was there a lack of communication between those supervising and the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you would disagree with this finding of the commission too. Since, in item 4, they assert --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 20008 back on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In item 4, the commission asserts -- or actually finds that there was a total lack -- well, in English, we need page 11. And I believe it's the same page in the B/C/S version. So this is one of the conclusions of the commission. Number 4: "Total lack of communication between supervisors and between supervisors and volunteer personnel." You would disagree with this conclusion by the commission; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was total because how would we have ever gotten anything done?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I accept this answer. Would you agree with conclusion number 6 where it is stated: "Universal agreement on the alteration of reports and final opinion as to the cause and manner of death without consulting the prosecutor who had performed the post-mortem examination. This should not have been done."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this questions that been asked five times now, and the witness said that it was inappropriate to do it. And he added to that with concent, without consultation, therefore. So would you please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I thought we are in the field of conclusions now and it [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question at all arises whether we should ask the witness conclusions or opinions or whether should -- and to the extent we ask him about conclusions and opinions, it's pretty obvious, here and there, where it's divergent from what the committee concluded, and let that be some guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if the commission found that there was unnecessary haste in having certain grave-sites exhumed; and do you believe that it was done in a rush?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about. When you're talking about hate. But we didn't rush through these. We were very -- we did it, but we did very well. So I don't think we rushed through those. If you're an archaeologist you could stay for five -- you go back for five, six, seven, eight, nine years to dig a grave. We don't do that. We don't do that in forensics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In item 7, the commission found that there was little need for rapidity of some grave-site exhumations and only one exhumation should have been performed at one time. You would disagree with that as well, would you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only time there were two graves -- doing that had a separate team in Croatia and a separate team to finish up in Bosnia. Of -- I don't see it as a problem. Had very good people in both places. I was going to say if -- if -- in the United States if they had two or three homicides, they wouldn't wait to do one for another. They would go and do them probably much all at the same time. Send people to different places, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So was there rapidity or haste, or do you disagree with the conclusion of the commission? Do you believe there was no haste in the process of digging up the grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think we did it very well. And -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you take the time you thought you need to do it? That's the question, I think, Mr. Lukic would like to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's why we didn't do any more graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there any changing of bone position? And is it true that to a certain extent they were not protected after being dug up?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only ever time I had a problem with that was in Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since it was only the task the commission to reach search conclusions on Srebrenica exhumations, that is to say, the exhumations in Bosnia, in item 8, they assert that there was some validity to the charge of shifting and non-protection of the bones. You would disagree with this conclusion of the commission as well, as you have just stated?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: People at the -- at the grave and any time that we weren't there. There's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You would disagree with the conclusion, would you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is what one now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's number 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you, in your question, be clear about what is exactly to be understood under "shifting." It's unclear to me. I haven't read the whole of the report. I ... What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would rather ask the witness [Overlapping speakers] ... shifting. The bones -- the bones that moved from one location unprotected to another location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it means that. But if that is -- then please put the question in such a way that we perfectly understand what you consider to be shifting. Were bones moved from one exhumation, Mr. Lukic, to another, or is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The bones were moved from the location to the laboratory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can't do any useful post-mortems if you don't move the bones from the grave-site --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... unprotected and left somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, so shifting is now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The main part here is unprotected here. Whether it's -- of course there had to be moved and shifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently your question is not entirely clear to yourself as well. I take it that the bones were transported from one place to another, in order to perform the autopsies or the post-mortems. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for each grave we would have a place that we could lock up and have protected of anything we moved from the grave. They were zipped up, numbered, and then when we were done, we would take them all to the laboratory once we had done with the particular grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you aware what the committee's concerns were about the non-protection of bones, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not sure what I meant -- what that meant, I mean. When bones are exposed and were waiting overnight, they were -- would be covered with tarps and so other things could get in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would there be personnel to watch the site overnight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had -- we had -- we had individuals. We had people that are guarding the graves every night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want from this witness is to tell me if he agrees with this finding of the commission or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking -- the thing I'm trying to make clear to you is that by just reading a line I, at least, have difficulties in understanding exactly what shifting means in this context. So, therefore, for a witness to answer a question, it should be clear to him what is put to him and it may well be that the witness has a better understanding. That's the reason why I asked him whether he has any knowledge about these concerns. And then he answered questions of fact. And apparently, that's at least how I understand his answer, that he did not -- he was not aware of charges of -- or concerns about shifting, and that he described to us how the bones were protected. That's the factual question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm very satisfied when he confirms that something is wrong in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine what you like to hear from the witness. But I -- the Chamber is supervising the questioning of this witness, and we do it in the way as you at this moment experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you agree with the ninth conclusion of the commission, which reads: "There was too much subjectivity and not enough objectivity in the performance of the exhumations and post-mortem examinations."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand that particular statement, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you could make it concrete what that means exactly, subjectivity of exhumations or objectivity in the performance of exhumations. You could perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot either because if I compose this document, I would probably be able to do so. I don't know what they meant either [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, so neither does the Chamber, neither does Mr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I accept this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you plan and co-ordinate the anthropological and pathological investigations on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no pathologists on the ground at the graves, but I was in charge of the graves, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you plan and co-ordinate your activity with the pathologists?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We brought the bodies to the -- to the laboratory, and then they -- they could take over from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did overall work suffer due to a potential lack of planning and co-ordination with the pathologists?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, is it correct that you disagree with the conclusion number 10 of the commission, which reads, as you can see on the screen: "There was no attempt to schedule or co-ordinate anthropological and pathological investigations."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you telling me that something was written down so that somebody could read how to work or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the conclusions, the commission attempted to put forth the reasons for its conclusions and opinion at the end of the report. You told us just now that there were no problems on the ground, due do any kind of lack of planning and co-ordination with the pathologists. I accept that answer, and I'll move on. In the course of your work, were you bothered by the fact that there was some media presence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the -- the only time I ever had any sort of people that were taking photographs or anything like that, I had permission or I was asked by the Tribunal to let them on -- on the -- on the grave -- not on the grave, but on the area where we had -- we had a -- we had a pretty broad area of -- roped off so people can come in and our people would keep them out, not -- not our anthropologists, but the people we had there to guard the grave. And I think it only happened two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the amount of attention dedicated to the media did not affect your work; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't affect my work. I talked to them when I was asked to by the Tribunal, and, no, we had a very good -- we got along very good with them. We just had to explain what they could do and what they couldn't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that conclusion number 11 which is before you where it is stated that there was too much concern with regard to media involvement is inaccurate? Did you pay too much attention to the media? I believe you told us you did not.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could talk to them according to the Tribunal sometimes, and I did. And they didn't get on the grave. Only twice when the Tribunal told me I could allow them to come on. I got along very good with the -- the people, but this doesn't mean that I had to give them any of our secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to answer the question. Would you agree with this conclusion, or would you not agree with this conclusion by the commission?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I mean, they may have -- I think we had very good -- we were pretty strict about the media. And I don't know how they even get these ideas, so I have no idea where they come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This conclusion of the commission that there was too much concern with regard to media involvement, is it, in your view, accurate or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's an awful -- there was an awful lot of interest in these graves, and -- and what was going on. So they did -- they wrote an awful lot. I don't know if they didn't get it from us but they got a lot of information. They worked hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know of any other ways to put this: In the course of your work there, did you pay too much attention to the media?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If I understand it correctly, then this question has actually been put to the witness several times, and he's done his best to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. But I didn't get an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's still to be seen. If you give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, page 40, line 10, "... didn't affect my work." Isn't that an answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, some words were attributed to you, and I wanted to ask you if you would agree with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to see 65 ter 25677.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have been shown this book in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, just to jog your memory --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this at all, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just so that it's clear, it's not a book, it's a seminar that was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, seminar, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very precise then on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another document [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... what is before you on the screen at this moment, Dr. Haglund, seems to be a report on a seminar sponsored by the Crimes of War Project and The Freedom Forum, a seminar which took place, I don't know when, Mr. Lukic. Could you assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be December 2007, Mr. Lukic? That's at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I can see, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what appears from your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukic, you're asking questions about page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Four, yes. That's paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is all under the heading, as we see on the first page, Mr. Haglund, there is a heading which reads: From Rwanda to East Timor collecting physical evidence of war crimes. And you are the one reported to have spoken at that seminar. I don't even know whether this is an announcement of a seminar or a report of the seminar. Do you remember that you have been at a seminar in 2007 where you have lectured or given a presentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very likely that I was there. I don't remember this. I've written many, many papers and many, many chapters in books, and I have to read them again. I don't remember them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic will put some questions to you about what you purportedly would have presented there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to find whether this refers to Rwanda or Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's the heading on the first page. And I see no other heading on pages 2 and 3, so -- and it says from Rwanda to East Timor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 2, the last paragraph, it was talking about staffing and it's talking about Bosnia. Just to look at the -- the kind of staffing in Bosnia in 1996 as: "All told, I had about 100 people on the ground, about 50 at the time rotating through; that's 33 pathologist, 24 anthropologists." From the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read slowly so that the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait for the page to come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You're quoting from page ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The last paragraph on page 2, continuing on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please slowly read.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in Popovic trial, this gentleman was shown this passage, this quotation in regard of Bosnia, so [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he accepted that it was [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'm not a Judge in that case so I would like to understand what happens in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the quotation is on page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the quotation is about Bosnia. That's clear. Could you please slowly read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. It's paragraph 3. Can you blow it up for the doctor. Page 4, paragraph 3. The first part of paragraph -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. We're now on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four. Then I would have to ... Please continue. Meanwhile, I'll see whether the subject changes anywhere in between. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I quote: "I slow plate this one and that's one of the responses [sic] -- reasons," sorry, "I had a four-ring circus going on. I was going absolutely crazy here. But sometimes you're lucky and you have the resources you [sic] cover the grave and sometimes you are not."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, this description of yours, does it actually say that there was chaos in the field?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was just waiting to hear the end of the question, but prior to that, my friend represented that the witness, in Popovic, had attributed these comments to Bosnia which in fact is not the case. So I just want it to be clear for the witness before he answers the question. I can -- I don't want to read out his answer. I want him to have the opportunity to answer the question, but I just wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, can I read from the Popovic transcript so maybe the doctor can recall easier what he answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need 1D1158. So 1D1158, we need -- it's transcript from Popovic trial. We need page 18, but the second part attached says here. So it's second part. We need page number -- from transcript page number 8971. And then we need lines 5 to 15. Because I would start quoting -- it was quoted the same quotation from line 2, it's visible in this transcript, and the question was in line 5, says: "Q. Is that your statement, sir? "A. Absolutely. "Q. And that was your statement in regard to these digs in 1996 in Srebrenica; correct? "A. That was a characterisation of how, in a post-conflict environment, when are you doing these things, that's how you feel. Yes. And you have to regulate the pace of -- of the work. And sometimes you, um, ..." And goes on. I have it on page 19 and 20. It was pretty long answer. But it's obvious that it's in connection with Srebrenica and 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it says -- I've not seen that now. It's -- it says, "... in a post-conflict environment, when you're doing these things ..." It's an interpretation of the answer in relation to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, sir, do you remember today whether this statement of yours pertained to Bosnia; and if it did pertain to Bosnia, what did this mean, this four-ring circus? And in American English what is a three-ring circus mean?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Life can be a circus. It can be a four-ring circus. It can be a three-ring circus. Many things are going on at the same time. It seems like it is crazy. But when you start look into each one of those circles something is happening. You can work -- look at them at one time, but you keep going around and you -- and so that's -- that's sort of what life is like and that's what -- sort of what this was like. I didn't think I was crazy. I think -- it just was very, very busy. That's fine. I like to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic I'm looking at the clock. I think it's time for a break. Mr. Haglund, if you would follow the usher, we'll take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time to say something about Exhibit P997. Exhibit P997 contains two B/C/S translations, and the Registry is hereby instructed to remove the translation with ERN number R008-6180-B/C/ST.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In e-court, can we please have 65 ter 25679. It is a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were already asked at the Popovic trial whether you knew Elizabeth Neuffer. [In English] I don't know if I pronounced her name correctly.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know her. She was killed in Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked about one paragraph, and I'm going ask you about that. In English, we need page 17. Since it's double, we need the right-hand side, the second paragraph from the top of the page. In B/C/S, we need page 36, the middle of the page. So the late Ms. Neuffer wrote the following: [In English] "After the exhumations ended, several members of the team complained to Tribunal investigators that shortcuts had been taken that could compromise the evidence. Among the complaints, other than Haglund's management style, were that the graves had not been made secure. Animals had raided some of them, dragging off body parts. Other allegations centred on administrative sloppiness; some bodies and their parts had been wrongly labelled. Fearful that Defence attorneys in the case might have been handed a powerful weapon, the Tribunal and its lawyers launched an internal inquiry." Do you know what the source of information is, the information included by this lady in her book?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: She used to call me a lot to ask me questions, and I wouldn't give her answers. So she was a very good friend of mine but when people are writing books they write what they want to write. I don't have anything to do with that. I don't believe all of this, and I -- I loved a lot of -- the part of the book but that's about all I could say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you tell us when the book was published? I may have missed it on the first page, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have only two pages with me. Actually, the first page, and I cannot see when it was published. But we will -- we would probably be able to provide Your Honours with that date soon, in 15 minutes probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second part or, rather, the last part of this assertion that this was an internal inquiry, do you know how this commission was made up, or do you not have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we've been talking about today is not really considered an internal inquiry, right? I don't know. She found out this -- she -- she worked for newspapers all of her life. She was good at finding things. I have no idea where she would get this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are not going to dwell on this any longer. Now I'd like us to go back to 65 ter 20008. We need page 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one thing. The internal inquiry, as far as you understand matters, the witness partially can't help us, but is that the same as the San Antonio matter, which of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, then it's clear to me that there was only one and not another one because the San Antonio was not entirely internal. Thank was my --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll see why I think it was internal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And only that I was just helped by my colleague sitting in the back that this book, "The Key to my Neighbour's House" was published in November 2002, although it was reprint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a reprint.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Reprint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, I was interested in -- if you asked about the sources if it was long after the San Antonio report had been published then it may shed a different light on the sources for the ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, under Roman numeral VII towards the bottom of the page, you will see this note, nota bene, NB. What is written here is as follows: "Preserve old materials and have it available to the entire court in order allay the charge of conspiracy or collusion. Develop a series of questions to counteract any cross-examination attack on the reports. Consider using outside forensic experts."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is this that you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's on the bottom the page, Doctor. It's under NB.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can that be blown up? Too much?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That happens if the witness is touching the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that. Thank you. This was a suggestion in that query that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this position taken by the committee obviously shows that the committee is interested --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a lot of this -- okay. I think a lot of it that they say has been -- had been done but they wanted make sure that this is in their report because they were doing what should happen in a situation like this, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Question though --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to hear your question. I didn't hear any question in relation to that nota bene.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
