utterances.text: My question, Doctor, is: Do you know who formulated this position of the commission which is obviously aimed at preventing the Defence from challenging, in cross-examination, the findings of your work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they do. That's what they expect other people to do. I think that's what's expected here too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you know who formulated this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think there was a group of people there doing it. And they do it at theirs. We try to do it as much as possible too, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Lukic, I object against the way in which you characterise what is said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What would you ... I think it's clear that it's -- I'll follow -- I have some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no way that these recommendations are aimed at preventing the Defence for challenging in cross-examination. It rather seems that if there is a challenging cross-examination, where there are flaws, to prepare for the proper answers or at least some answers to that, not to prevent them from challenging it. It's a mischaracterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your questioning before this commission, did you gain the impression that this was precisely the task of the commission --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- to make it impossible to relativise the cross-examination and the evidence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- could you repeat that whole thing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the members of the Chamber is trying to get the power back on his computer and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Disappeared for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should we call a technician?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we're close to a solution. The usher is thanked for his assistance. It has been repaired. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were all distracted by efforts of Judge Moloto to get his power back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you agree, Doctor, that the work of this commission was actually aimed in its entirety at making it impossible to relativise the report in any way through cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what happens in the United States at -- at -- at courts. It happens all over the world. I'm sure that these gentlemen and gentle ladies, here, same as you, you do the same thing. This was something that wasn't being done. This is something that happens everywhere. A lot of these things when I look at them everybody does that. They just are confirming, you know, what things should be done. Doesn't mean that people aren't doing things properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a bit unclear when you refer to "this" various times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- the question was whether the aim of the commission was entirely at making it impossible to relativise the report in whatever way during cross-examination. Was that the aim of the committee to make that impossible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But I think when -- when you first are under the command of these -- not in the command. You're not under command. But they try to cover as much stuff as you could explain so that they put out of the way with these gentlemen and gentle ladies need to ask questions about. That's the way I understand it. I think it happens everywhere in all courts, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, after the session of this commission, you no longer went to Bosnia ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was done there, yes. Pretty much. Not all. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to Dr. Kirschner? Was he dismissed from that job?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was done with it. I believe he was done with the job at that point. I can't remember -- I don't remember actually when this was done, if there was still work that we were doing because I think I was in Africa at the time, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now we're going to move on to Rwanda and your work in Rwanda. That was mentioned yesterday. The Court in Rwanda in the Rutaganda case rejected your scientific approach and your scientific work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Judgement was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you apply the same methods in Rwanda and in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same -- same way we went about things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that case, in the Rutaganda case that is, you established the age of the killed person; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something: Do you think that you made a mistake in the Rutaganda case?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I made a mistake in the Rutaganda case, but I think a lot of the remains that we exhumed had nothing to do with that. But we were just asked to dig those graves, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that mistakes were made in the exhumations in Bosnia and in the processing of the exhumed parts?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I -- that I can remember. I don't think that -- I think we did well. It was the first time it was done on, and it was done well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were any mistakes made by the pathologists?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your work in Bosnia, did you make any distinction in terms of whether someone had been killed in fighting or executed or whether someone was a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were people that were taken away from Srebrenica. I don't know if they fought -- whether there. I have no idea, but they were -- they were actually -- they were killed. They were killed and they were not fighting in a -- with other people. They were just killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D1153 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence counsel kindly speak into the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're invited to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll move closer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see a document containing names. It seems to be a mutant of sorts between English and B/C/S contained in the same table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Out of caution, we should not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not broadcast. I was just warned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will not refer to the name and it should not be broadcast outside the courtroom. But we're interested in the eighth name from the bottom. The person in question was registered under protocol number 68/02 in the reports. It is reported that the remains were found in the Cerska grave-site. At the same time, we have the same person registered by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina - that is to say, the Muslim army - as someone who was killed on 10 January 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could it be made clear for the record what exactly this document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the document which will not be shown is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was used by my colleague Ivetic a few days ago. And I think you got explanation from him at the time or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just say what it is, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's part -- part of an expert expertise -- one of expert testifying in front of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just make the record clear. It's a table that is part of Radovanovic, his annex 3, which was a Defence expert in a prior case before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just kindly ask to see page 3 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, Doctor, all this list, it concerns people killed before July 1995, I'm only showing you two of them, one in connection of Cerska, and the other one in connection of Branjevo Military Farm. So, here, you'll see the fourth name from the top is in connection to Branjevo Military Farm. It has registration number 9295/07. And according to the Army of B and H records, this person was killed on 22nd April 1994. So do you have any explanation how was it possible that all these persons were killed in 1995, according to you, and still we can find it in the records of Army of B and H, that, according to their records, these persons were killed in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you mentioning that I have their names somewhere? If it was, it would be something that we found on the body. We did not identify these people. You're going to have to deal with the people that actually ended up doing the -- the identifications. I had nothing to do with the identifications, only giving them information that we had found on bodies, and blah blah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm telling your is -- or what I'm trying to tell you is that according to ICP records --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- those persons were exhumed, the first one from Cerska and the second one from Branjevo Military Farm.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You talk to them about the identification then. I have no -- I don't want to get involved in this because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, don't you think that is a question relevant, in fact, to ICMP and not this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- I think what Mr. Lukic would like to know, Mr. Haglund, and if you know anything about it, tell us, if you don't know anything about it, tell us as well, whether you would know what could possibly explain that there's a divergence between the date on which the body was reported to be exhumed and another register which says that that person had died already a year before that, whether you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answers the question. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, would you allow for the possibility today in your testimony that the graves contained the bodies of those who were executed, as well as of those killed in combat, not only in 1995 but also in the years previous? Do you allow for that possibility or can you exclude that possibility based on the scientific methods you applied?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's look at the Cerska grave. Okay? These people that weren't -- they weren't fighting. They were lined up along the road and killed. Period. They were killed there. They weren't fighting with anybody, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, was this person, too, a combatant who was registered by the Army of BiH as having been killed on 10 January 1994? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half the way to the person is identified. Then we could tell that. If they came from that grave, that's when they were killed. They were all killed at the same time. I don't have an answer to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. And your assertion also applies to the person on page 3, from the Branjevo Military Farm, registration number 929507 was also killed like others in July 1995. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same situation. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if I received an answer in terms of whether you distinguished between combatants and civilians and if you did make an attempt to distinguish between them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were buried and they were killed and buried. They weren't fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with those killed in combat? Did you have information that people were being killed during the breakthrough? Where were such corpses of Muslim fighters buried when they were killed in an attempt of breakthrough, through VRS territory from Srebrenica to Tuzla? Did they vanish? Did someone hide them, bury them? Do you have any sort of knowledge in that regard?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court 65 ter 2555, which is a Prosecution Exhibit. [In English] Is it with three 5s? Two 5s? 25555. Actually four 5s. Sorry. That is it. [Interpretation] Just to let you in on the context, as you can see, it is an UN document, Sector North-East Tuzla, B and H, civil affairs. The date is the 17th of July, 1995. That is to say, from the time of events. On page 4 in the B/C/S and page 2 in the English, we find the part I'd like to focus our attention on. We need the last bullet point of item 1. Can we zoom in. 1

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is reported, as you can see, on the 17th of July, 1995, as follows. I'll quote: [In English] "Up to 3.000 were killed on the way mostly by mines and BSA engagements. Unknown others were captured. Some committed suicide. Unknown others went to Zepa." [Interpretation] Doctor, did anyone from the UN, be it a representative of the Tribunal or a different representative of the UN in Bosnia and Herzegovina tell you that there were such people who were killed in combat during the column breakthrough from Srebrenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read about that. I know about that. But ICRC, when the women came across, they would report that people were missing. And I don't know if they told how they were killed. And -- and -- and then ICRC would go and tell the families, yeah, they were dead. How they found that out, they didn't know. And we closed them down because they were -- they were actually saying some people that were dead that weren't dead, and so people they didn't know were dead. We stopped them from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it is in dispute that there were those killed, the Prosecutor's Office does not deny that there were people killed in combat. Could you have ascertained that in any way? Did you exhume a single individual who was killed in combat in the process of the column breaking through from Srebrenica to Tuzla? Did you find a single case like that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea that they were -- that they weren't in combat. I know that. Okay? Unless -- unless they'd been in combat and then added to the grave at the same time the people were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were shooting -- if they were having a conflict, somebody shot them in the back, I have no idea. But I have nothing to do with this thing about the ICRC mis -- misnaming people that were dead and not. We didn't know. So we had to wait until it was over. And ... I didn't do the -- the identifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is why I'm asking you this. Based on scientific proof, can you exclude the possibility that in the graves there were the bodies of both those executed and those killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question already. He said what he observed was a typical picture of people lined up and then killed, but that he could not exclude that some other bodies were added in the same grave. That's what I heard you say, Mr. Haglund. Did I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- it's possible, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Unless they'd been in combat and then added to the grave at the same time the people were killed there." So he has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have an explanation as to where those killed in combat were buried, if they were not in the same graves with those executed? Did you reach any conclusions in the course of your work or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, same comment. You've asked this question. The witness even raised his hands and said, I've got no idea. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Popovic trial, you were asked about something, and I will read it out as we are nearing the end. Please do bear with me for a little longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need 1D1161. I apologise. We need 1D1158, the second part in e-court, the attached part. Pages 30 and 31, which should correspond to transcript page 8983, spilling over to 8984.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are interested in line 22, towards the bottom of the page: [In English] "Q. All right. Down on the fifth line, after the parentheses, it says: 'Accepting support directly from national governments would compromise the perception of independence and, consequently, their credibility.'" On the next page is recording your answer as: "Yes. "Q. Okay. "A. It could, yes. "Q. It could. "A. Yes." Now we have to go to line 10. And there we can find the question. I quote: "Don't you think that accepting money from the Office of the Prosecutor on a criminal case does the same -- has the same effect? "A. I don't know if the Physicians for Human Rights got any money from the Office of the Prosecutor. "Q. No, but you did, didn't you? "A. Yes. Yes, I was employed by them."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Let us ascertain something that has been established previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just try to understand. I -- I re-read the question -- the answer. You were asked whether accepting money from the Office of the Prosecutor in a criminal case would have the same -- and reference is made, compromising effect. Your answer was: "I don't know if the Physicians for Human Rights got any money from the Office of the Prosecutor ..." And then the question was: "No, but you did, didn't you? " The answer was: "Yes. Yes, I was employed by them." Was that a reference to the Office of the Prosecutor, that you were employed by them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Tribunal was paying me for doing the exhumations, the individuals with PHR that came, the physicians and that, I believe they donate -- I believe they donated their time but they were paid enough to eat and to get here and get back home, et cetera. These are people that, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you were paid by the Tribunal, you said. Were you -- did you have a labour contract or was it services rendered? On what basis were you paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what they would call it. I think you would have to ask possibly the individuals here or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But were you on the payroll receiving salary from the Tribunal or were you hired to do a job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was hired to do a job, and it took two and a half years to finish it when you get all the records from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the parties could agree on what the basis exactly was of the employment or perhaps Mr. McCloskey would even know and could tell us immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it's an SSA which is a contract for a special work for an expert. But I can check into that. That I don't recall. But I'm pretty sure that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties agree on that that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can clarify further and I think it -- we have it confirmed previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Does that mean that there's no dispute about it? Then, of course, the question is what -- the questions are aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask my questions [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the questions are relevant and if the questions are on matters in dispute then of course you are fully free to ask questions. I'm just inquiring whether there's any dispute about those matters so as not to lose time unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will finish in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, sir, you were actually hired and contacted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, before we move on to the next question, the portion read out by my learned friend which began on transcript page 8983 from the Popovic case was a question about getting support directly from national governments. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, if I may go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And the answer that we stopped as was, no -- which we just read, "... but didn't you?" Answer, "Yes, yes, I was employed by them." And the witness actually continues with his answer on line 17. We're talking here about NGOs accepting money not -- not forensic experts being paid for a job. And I think the entirety of the witness's answers should be in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are two issues. First, what the facts were. Second, what judgement or opinion you could have as to compromising. Part of that testimony is whether it compromised, yes or no, which is judgement an opinion rather than anything else. You can ask a witness whether he felt to be under pressure. That's factual. But let's try to stay away from judgement and let's focus on facts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, you were hired by Mr. Goldstone - correct? - who at the time was the Prosecutor both for Rwanda and The Hague Tribunal. You worked for the Rwanda Tribunal and then he told you to go to the locations in Bosnia to continue your work. Is that how your deployment to Bosnia actually took place?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a long discussion about this in the preceding case and I tried to cut it short concerning this topic. If I can have a minute, I believe I may be finished with my questions. Let me just try to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor thank you for answering our questions. That was all we had for you. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And have a good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Same to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at a point where we take a break, but we'll not do that before you have informed us, Ms. Hasan, whether there's any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I do have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how much time those questions would take? If it's more than three, four, or five minutes, we would take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It would be more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the witness is invited to follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, during yesterday's testimony, and that was at transcript page 14952, at lines 3 to 4, you were asked a question about working under Dr. Kirschner. Do you recall -- do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was there, yeah. He was, yeah --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Right. And -- and you spoke about it a little bit today as well, about the type of determinations of age and the -- the measurements of bones that were also done by the anthropologist to assists the pathologists in their work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you just help us a little bit more in relation to how it was that the anthropologists contributed to the work that the pathologists were doing?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would clean the bones. They'd do the -- the aging. They'd measure the stature of the individual and of -- and then they would do a lot of things about some of the individual bones that they were trying to match with the individual it belonged to. Some of the -- some of the graves, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was there any reconstruction of bones done by the anthropologist to also assist the pathologist?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. And they also -- after the examination of the clothing was done, they would clean them off and wash them. And so that the families would be able to have them in a decedent shape.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And would the anthropologist also -- did they have any role in the analysis of the skeletal remains and the injuries to those remains?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they worked together with the pathologist on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you just elaborate a little bit more on that, how that happened?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with the bone?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Not with the -- the [indiscernible] and they'd help. They'd -- well, we had a -- the doctors from very many countries and they had never worked with anthropologists before and so they assisted them in what they're finding and how they find it, and then they were kind of excited about learning about those things.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, sorry, was the anthropologist assisting the doctors? Do I understand you correctly, or was that the other way around?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they -- yeah, they assisted the doctor, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were also asked yesterday at transcript page 14962, approximately at lines 19 to 25, about the positioning of some bodies that were in the Nova Kasaba 2 grave and that they were in kneeling positions, some of them, and some were in sitting positions.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we call up Exhibit P1834 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1384"] MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in the course of answering that question you refer to that there were some photographs that showed this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 32. And since it's just a photograph, probably the English version will do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So can you tell us that -- first about the -- the picture you see on the top of that page?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You can see the individual's face down and their hands are tied behind their back, sort of commingled with other individuals too. These are complete bodies that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak in the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund, you've heard the request.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like me to repeat what I said? Okay. We have an individual on other -- other individuals, number 14, and he has his -- his wrist tied behind his back.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us whether or not this was an individual who was in the types of positions you referred to in a sitting or kneeling position?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was what grave you got this from?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This is from your Nova Kasaba report and it's grave 2, it says on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is that one grave. Yes, he was shot there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could just --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fell forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we just turn back one page.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what we're looking at here. We see -- we see some numbers there with the number 14 in the top right-hand corner of the page. It depict the person we just saw in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That person fell forward after he had been shot, basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And this shows -- does this depict the bodies that you were trying to explain to us where some of them were kneeling, some of them sitting, some of them were laying over and that they fell on top of each other?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do we --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. Mr. Lukic, the cross-examination has triggered no need for further questions? Mr. Haglund, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, both by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like -- I like your group, yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, I think that there are still three remaining MFIs, that is P1831, P1833, and P1834. I think the parties have already expressed themselves on it. The Chamber has delayed the decision until after cross-examination. Is there anything the parties think they should add to what they had submitted already?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not in relation to that. I just have two points. Just earlier now I think the exhibit I referred to was incorrectly recorded. It's at page -- transcript page 69, line 4. And it's says "could we call up P1384 MFI." It should be P1834 MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in addition to that, Your Honours, we are prepared to offer in the -- the cross-examination that was conducted by counsel in the Popovic case as well as the direct. If that would -- if the direct would assist in understanding the cross-examination, the Prosecution is prepared to offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any response to that offer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we respond tomorrow during the housekeeping session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may consider the situation. Then as far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan has put the right number on the record but it was not recorded. The document was P1834. Please correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we move to the decision on the MFI'd, P1831, P1833 and P1834. The Chamber delayed the decision. Any further observations by the parties? If not, P1831, P1833, and P1834 are admitted into evidence. Then before we move to the next witness, I would like to use the opportunity to read -- to deliver two decisions. The first one is a -- concerns the Chamber's consideration of the Prosecution's proposal to call a legal expert. On the 18th of February of this year, the Prosecution made an oral proposal and circulated a related memo with the intention of developing an agreed list of legal documents relevant to the case and identifying an international law expert to assist the Chamber in clarifying the legal status and obligations arising from such documents. In response to this proposal, at transcript page 8874, the Chamber noted that lack of clarity sometimes results from the examination of witnesses as opposed to the legal understanding of the Chamber, and that the Chamber is primarily tasked with establishing legal issues. The Chamber nonetheless invited the parties to prepare submissions on the matter for it to consider in determining whether a legal expert would be necessary. The Defence filed its submission on the 1st of March, 2013, opposing the Prosecution's proposal on the grounds that use of a legal expert is contrary to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and invades the purview of the chamber. The Prosecution did not make any additional submissions. The Chamber is not persuaded that it should deviate from its original position expressed in court on the 18th of February, and, therefore, does not see the necessity of calling a legal expert. The Prosecution is instructed to file the related memorandum for completeness of the case record. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The next decision is a decision on two outstanding issues with regard to Witness Martin Bell which are, first, the admission of his consolidated witness statement and the remaining exhibits associated to it; as well as, two, the admission of five video-clips on which the witness gave comments in a comment chart. In its Rule 92 ter motion concerning Witness Martin Bell of the 21st of December, 2012, the Prosecution tendered one consolidated witness statement of Martin Bell dated the 8th of March, 2010, currently marked for identification as Exhibit P832, together with 44 associated exhibits. Following the testimony of Witness Bell on the 31st of January and the 1st of February, 2013, the Prosecution, on the 18th of February, submitted a revised list of the remaining associated exhibits which were not yet addressed in court and had not yet been tendered into evidence. This revised list contained a remainder of 38 associated exhibits to the consolidated witness statement of Witness Bell. On the 11th of February of 2013, the Defence filed additional submissions as to the associated exhibits and statement of Witness Bell, followed by the Prosecution's response of the 18th of February of this year. The Prosecution's request for leave to exceed the word limit is hereby granted. Considering the parties' discussion relating to certain paragraphs of the consolidated witness statement of Witness Bell which deal with Zvornik and the paramilitary unit of alleged JCE member Zeljko Raznjatovic, commonly referred to as Arkan, the Chamber recalls its decision pursuant to Rule 73 bis (D) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the 2nd of December, 2001. By this decision, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's request for reduction of its case while at the same time noting that it does not strictly prohibit the Prosecution from presenting evidence on incidents the Prosecution has proposed to remove, if it considers this necessary to prove an element of a charged count. The Chamber instructed the Prosecution in such instances to clearly indicate any such proposed evidence in its Rule 65 ter filings and to explain its specific relevance to the Prosecution's case. Evidence relating to Zvornik is one of those instances. With regard to the Defence's argument that the topic of Zvornik was not noticed in Witness Bell's Rule 65 ter summary, the Chamber, at the outset, notes that the Defence was, in fact, able to cross-examine Witness Bell on the disputed paragraphs of his consolidated statement. This can be found at transcript pages 7906 to 7913. Moreover, the Chamber has provided guidance on the 24th of August, 2012, which can be found at transcript page 1639, stating that even though it is preferable that the Prosecution indicates its intention to elicit evidence on a certain topic already in the Rules 65 ter summary, if such an indication is included in the Rule 92 ter statement, it provides sufficient notice to the Defence. For these reasons, the Chamber admits into evidence the redacted version of Witness Bell's consolidated witness statement, currently marked for identification as Exhibit P832. The Chamber will now turn to its decision on the remaining associated exhibits. As stated earlier, these concern 38 remaining associated documents, out of which one, namely, Rule 65 ter number 10028, in the meantime, has been admitted through another witness as Exhibit P1066 and therefore does not require a further decision by the Chamber. Out of the remaining 37 documents, 35 are short video-clips; the other two being a map, Rule 65 ter number 08297; and a short newspaper article from the "New York Times" on the situation in Zepa in early 1993, Rule 65 ter 19311. Both of these documents are inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's testimony and therefore meet the test applied by the Chamber in its oral decision of the 22nd of November, 2012, on the admission of associated exhibits related to Witness Tucker. The Chamber therefore admits these two documents into evidence as associated exhibits to the consolidated witness statement of Witness Bell and requests the Registry to assign exhibit numbers for them. With regard to the 35 remaining associated video-clips, the Chamber notes that while none of them meet the test applied for Witness Tucker, it considers that admitting them into evidence will help the Chamber to visualise the evidence provided by Witness Bell in his statement. For these reasons, the Chamber admits into evidence the remaining 35 associated video-clips bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 22328, 22353, 22360, 22414A, 22509A through F and J, 22531A [Realtime transcript read in error "225301"] through D and E, 22565A through D, 22619B through E, 22625B, C, and E through J, 22630B and D, as well as 22646B and C, and requests the Registry to assign exhibit numbers to them. Turning to the second issue in relation to the admission of the remaining underlying video-clips to Witness Bell's comments chart admitted as Exhibit P833 on the 31st of January, 2013, the Chamber notes at the outset that out of the nine underlying video-clips on the chart, the Prosecution withdrew its request to tender the two clips bearing Rule 65 ter number 22630E and 22784C. Furthermore, two clips were admitted into evidence during the testimony of Witness Bell as Exhibits P834 and P841. With regard to the remaining five video-clips, the Chamber notes that Witness Bell, during his testimony, affirmed the accuracy of his comments made on the chart on which he identified the voices of either himself or of direct colleagues in relation to the respective clips. This can be found at transcript page 7815. And having analysed the documents, the Chamber considers that they meet the standard of reliability necessary for admission. The Defence has not objected to the admission of these video-clips. And, in light of the foregoing, the Chamber admits Rule 65 ter numbers 22625K, 22688A, as well as 22784A, B, and D into evidence and requests the Registry to assign exhibit numbers to them. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Madam Registrar, you're invited to assign those numbers in a memo which is to be filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record I would like to correct one number which was incorrectly recorded. It is page 76, line 9, there we find 225301. Instead of that it should be 22531 without a zero in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have ten minutes left which is not much. I could deal with a few matters which would not take the full ten minutes but perhaps better than to call the next witness at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that would be a good path, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially since we'll not immediately start tomorrow morning at 9.30 with the examination of the witness. Then let me just look what I still have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like first to deal with the Chamber's outstanding decision on the document bearing 65 ter number 09670 in relation to the witness statement of Witness Smith admitted as P785. Following the Chamber's decision on the remaining associated exhibits of Witness Smith which was issued orally on the 15th of July of this year, the Chamber yesterday received the outstanding clarification of the Prosecution in relation to the document bearing 65 ter number 09670. At transcript page 14549, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that the document relates to the first sentence of paragraph 130 of the witness statement of Witness Smith, which was previously admitted as P785. The Chamber has reviewed the respective paragraph and considers the document to be an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's testimony and, therefore, admits the document 65 ter number 09670 into evidence. And, Madam Registrar, would you please assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09670 receives number P1849, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1849 is admitted into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on that matter. I would like to deal now with a follow-up on a decision, a decision of the 19th of October, 2012, wherein under Rule 92 bis the Chamber admitted into evidence redacted versions of two photographs of a collapsed house and instructed the Prosecution to upload these redacted versions into e-court. The redacted photographs were subsequently assigned exhibit numbers P392 and P393. The Chamber also invited the Prosecution to provide a full translation of the redacted text accompanying the photographs and then seek the replacement of the exhibits. On the 29th of October, 2012, the Prosecution submitted fully translated versions of the two photographs through an informal communication. On the 30th of October, through an informal communication, the Chamber informed the parties that it considered this submission as a request for replacement. The Defence did not respond to this request. The Chamber has considered the fully translated versions of the two photographs and accepts that they replace the redacted versions initially admitted. The Chamber notes that e-court already contains the fully translated versions so no further instructions are necessary. Then the last issue concerns Exhibit P1495. On the 19th of July, the Chamber admitted P1495 into evidence. It appears, however, that translation errors pointed out in court on the 28th of May, 2013, at transcript pages 11636 through 11638 have not been rectified. Can the Prosecution confirm that the English translation of P1495 has, by now, been verified? You may not know the answer by heart, immediately, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He is looking at Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll need to check into that a bit -- a bit more, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have not verified it, you're invited to do so. And if it has been verified, we'll then further proceed to replacement. Those were the matters I had on my agenda. Mr. Lukic, can already anything be said about the presence of Mr. Mladic tomorrow during the housekeeping session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He will be with us tomorrow morning. So nothing has to be arranged extraordinary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good to hear. We'll adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 25th of July, 2013, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of July, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
